results.title: Why don't Bayesian methods require multiple testing corrections? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Why don't Bayesian methods require multiple testing corrections? Andrew Gelman wrote an extensive article on why Bayesian AB testing doesn't require multiple hypothesis correction: Why We (Usually) Don’t Have to Worry About Multiple Comparisons, 2012. I don't quite understand: why don't Bayesian methods require multiple testing corrections? In the Bayesian world, the prior "pulls back" on any point estimates, and the updated posterior distribution applies to inference at any time and requires no complex sample space considerations. If we use Bayesian estimation/testing instead, having some prior (around 0?) for all comparisons, then yes the prior will shrink the posteriors toward zero, but we would still have randomly varying posteriors and/or Bayes factors and will probably have some cases out of 1000 that will look like "substantial" effects, even when true effects are all zero. No. This particular suggestion by Gelman (who acknowledges the issue with looking at too many different things and then too easily wrongly concluding that you see something for some of them - in fact one of his pet topics on his blog) is distinct from a the extreme alternative viewpoint that holds that Bayesian methods do not need to account for multiplicity, because all that matters are your likelihood (and your prior). $\begingroup$ (+1) To my knownledge in expect in a few case (e.g. undimensional with matching prior) Bayesian inference does not offer any control on type 1 error rate. So Multiple Testing Correction in the Bayesian setting cannot be IHMO thought as a correction for type-1 error. As pointed out by the other answer, this correction does not offer any control on type I error but in most cases, Bayesian method does not offer any such control even at the single inference scale and correction for multiple comparison must be thought differently in the Bayesian setting. The whole multiple comparisons doesn't need to be dealt with, because the Bayesian approach is incorporating the *information that leads us to worry into the prior and/or likelihood*. Why is there usually no correction for multiple comparisons in Bayesian statistics? 1") Can Bayesian credible intervals adjust for multiple testing? 8") Why is a "Correction" Required in Multiple Hypothesis Testing?

results.content: It has also been argued that WAIC is a more fully Bayesian approach (compared to DIC) and is suitable for singular models, such as LMMs for longitudinal data when the random effects are considered as parameters in the model [18]. Whether the marginal or the conditional version of the LMM is fitted to the data, it has an impact on the performance of the model selection criteria even when the conditional and marginal LMM essentially lead to the same model. As will be shown in Section 5, these two versions of the model selection criteria are associated with different aims: cDIC (and similarly for cPSBF and cWAIC) considers the random effects as parameters of focus in the model whereas for mDIC (also mPSBF and mWAIC) the population of random effects represents the focus. In practice, this implies for mixed effects models that the conditional selection criteria evaluate the performance of the model when the population consists of all (future) measurements of the subjects included in the current study, while the marginal version of the criteria measures the performance of the model for all (future measurements of all) future subjects from the same population. The first set of simulations makes use of the classical model LMM assumptions, i.e. when the random effects and measurement errors have a normal distribution. To avoid specifying the marginal model in the estimation process, an R function was implemented, which computes the marginalized version of DIC, PSBF and WAIC for a Gaussian, skew-normal and skew-t distribution of the random effects and measurement error. Simulation study 1: performance of the Bayesian model selection criteria for the Potthoff & Roy data set. Simulation study 1: performance of the Bayesian model selection criteria for the Jimma infant growth data set. It is interesting to note that the conditional criteria select C5 (the model that assumes a skew-normal distribution for the random effects) in about 65% while the marginal criteria choose C5 in about 2%. We also assessed the performance of the model selection criteria when the normality assumption for the random effects and measurement errors are relaxed. Simulation study 3: performance of the Bayesian model selection criteria for gamma(2,1) for random error and for random effect.

results.title: Multiple changepoint detection and Bayesian model selection
results.content: We model this problem as a switching (inhomogeneous) Poisson process: at each point in time, the number of events that occur is Poisson distributed, and the _rate_ of events is determined by the unobserved system state z t:. To model the evolution of states over time, we'll define a simple transition model p(z t|z t−1): let's say that at each step we stay in the previous state with some probability p, and with probability 1−p we transition to a different state uniformly at random. Note that the latent states in this model are identifiable only up to permutation, so the rates we recovered are in a different order, and there's a bit of noise, but generally they match pretty well. Plotting the posterior probabilities, we recover the model's "explanation" of the data: at which points in time is each state active? We can view this as a case of Bayesian model selection: we have a set of candidate models, each with a different number of latent states, and we want to choose the one that is most likely to have generated the observed data.
